title: Late Cenozoic Ice Age begins on Antarctica

facts.text: Ice began to build up on Antarctica about 33.9 million years ago, opening the Late Cenozoic Ice Age that still continues.
The Eocene–Oligocene boundary marks Earth's switch from its last greenhouse climate to the present icehouse.
Falling carbon dioxide, past a tipping point of about 600 ppm, was the main driver of Antarctic glaciation.
For the first time in the Phanerozoic, both poles fell well below freezing.
Ice-rafted debris shows glaciers had also appeared on Greenland by the start of the Oligocene.

title: First ground sloths, soon in the Caribbean

facts.text: The earliest unambiguous ground-sloth fossils come from the early Oligocene.
Ground sloths had reached the Caribbean by 31 million years ago, shown by a femur from Puerto Rico.
Megatheriids, the family of the later giant ground sloths, appeared in South America about 30 million years ago.

title: Alps rise rapidly

facts.text: The Alps rose rapidly as Africa pushed north into Eurasia, isolating the remnants of the Tethys Sea.
Most Alpine mountain building took place in the Oligocene and Miocene.
From about 30 to 10 million years ago, shallow-marine and continental sediment filled the Molasse basin north of the Alps.

title: Andes become a major mountain chain

facts.text: The Andes first became a major mountain chain as subduction turned more directly into the coast.
About 30 million years ago, the Andean orogeny was rearranged on a continental scale.
Changes in subduction boosted volcanism, and the Western Cordillera of the Central Andes began to grow.

title: Carnivorans become top predators

facts.text: Carnivorans, led by the cat-like nimravids, took over the top-predator roles held in the Eocene by oxyaenids and mesonychians.
Dogs, nimravids, bears, weasels and raccoons began to replace the creodonts in the Old World.

title: Early desmostylians

facts.text: Early desmostylians, such as Behemotops, are known from the Oligocene.
These marine mammals reached their highest diversity in the Late Oligocene, with about nine species.

title: Grasslands begin to spread as forests retreat

facts.text: Grasslands expanded around the world while tropical broadleaf forests shrank back to the equatorial belt.
By the early Oligocene, North American and Eurasian tropical forests had given way to dry woodland and wide grasslands.
Grasses spread out of their wetland-edge habitats into open country; in South America the cooler climate spread savanna.
Falling carbon dioxide favored C4 photosynthesis, typical of grasses, yet even by the epoch's end grass was not common enough for modern savannas.
Cooling and spreading grassland favored the evolution of larger mammals.

title: Obik Sea retreats, joining Europe and Asia

facts.text: The Obik Sea, which had separated Europe from Asia, retreated early in the Oligocene and left a lasting land connection.
Falling sea level closed the Turgai Strait across it, opening Europe to Asian mammals.

title: Oi-2 glaciation and record sea-level fall

facts.text: Several pulses of glaciation struck in the middle Oligocene, around the Oi-2 oxygen isotope shift.
Growing Antarctic ice caused the largest sea-level drop of the past 100 million years, about 75 metres.
Rivers cut into exposed continental shelves, leaving gaps in marine rock records around the world.
Lesser turnovers of animal life coincided with the Oi-2 event.

title: Paratethys becomes a giant anoxic sea

facts.text: In the Oligocene a northern arm of the Tethys, the Paratethys, covered much of central and eastern Europe.
A sea-level drop and the uplift of Alpine mountain chains partly cut it off from the Tethys.
Poorly connected to the world ocean, it became stratified and turned into a giant anoxic sea.
Sand from rising mountains buried organic matter in the Maykop Suite, now a source of hydrocarbons around the Black Sea.
The Menilite Formation preserves its deep-sea fish and microbial mats.

title: Grande Coupure: Asian mammals replace Europe's

facts.text: Around 33.5 million years ago, Europe's mammal fauna turned over sharply as Asian species arrived; the French name means 'great break'.
Asian animals replaced most European mammals, except some endemic rodent and marsupial families.
Falling sea level closed the Turgai Strait, letting Asian rhinos and ruminants into Europe, where they drove native species extinct.
Before it, Europe was dominated by native artiodactyls, palaeothere perissodactyls, and adapid and omomyid primates.
The break brought widespread extinction; the first Asian immigrants appear about 350,000 years later in northwest European records.

conflicts.note: Oligocene page places it at the start of the epoch

title: Atacama Desert begins to dry out

facts.text: A proto-Humboldt Current, set up with the Tasmania–Antarctic passage about 33 million years ago, began the Atacama's drying; it may be Earth's oldest desert.
Humid air was generally lacking there after 33 million years ago, apart from brief wetter spells.

title: Labrador Sea spreading stops; Eurekan orogeny ends

facts.text: About 33 million years ago, seafloor spreading in the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay ceased and shifted to the northeast Atlantic.
The end of spreading brought the Eurekan orogeny of the Arctic to a close.
Until then, Greenland had moved as a separate plate, drifting north and rotating anticlockwise.
By the late Oligocene the North America–Eurasia boundary ran along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, with Greenland rejoined to North America.

conflicts.note: Atlantic Ocean page: Labrador Sea spreading lasted until 36 Ma

title: Tasmanian Gateway opens between Australia and Antarctica

facts.text: The Tasman Gateway between Australia and Antarctica opened at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary, about 33 million years ago, bringing abrupt cooling.
Shallow channels south of Tasmania opened in the Eocene; deep-ocean routes followed from the mid Oligocene.
Australia had drifted slowly from Antarctica since the Jurassic; one estimate puts a deep channel in place by the end of the early Oligocene.
Southeastern Australia then became a land of high rainfall and swamps.

title: Haughton impact on Devon Island

facts.text: An impactor about 2 km wide struck Devon Island in Arctic Canada 31–32 million years ago.
It left a crater about 23 km across, exposing rock from as deep as 1,700 m.

contested_note: Its age has been revised several times: the Oligocene page calls it questionable and cites a 39-million-year Eocene age, while the crater's own page gives 31–32 million years.

facts.text: Aegyptopithecus, a howler-monkey-sized catarrhine predating the ape–Old World monkey split, lived in Egypt's Fayum about 30.2–29.5 million years ago.
Its Jebel Qatrani Formation spans the Eocene–Oligocene boundary and records tropical forests, swamps and rivers draining north into the Tethys Sea.
The formation holds over a dozen primate genera and early elephants such as Phiomia and Moeritherium, key to the early evolution of modern mammal groups.

title: Antarctic Circumpolar Current forms

facts.text: A steady current circling Antarctica probably did not form until about 30 million years ago.
Once the gateways opened, the current kept cold water circling Antarctica and strengthened the formation of Antarctic Bottom Water.
A shallow flow at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary may have started a proto-current, but it was too shallow for a true circumpolar current.
Deep-sea cores south of New Zealand show cold deep currents by the early Oligocene.
Fossil evidence places the current's full establishment about 23 million years ago, once the Drake Passage opened fully and the Tasman Gateway deepened.

contested_note: Its timing depends on the disputed opening of the Drake Passage, and how much it drove Oligocene cooling is debated.

facts.text: The brontotheres, large hoofed mammals, went extinct about 30 million years ago.

conflicts.note: Oligocene page places the extinction in the earliest Oligocene

facts.text: The Caspian Sea is estimated to be about 30 million years old.
Flood basalts poured across Ethiopia, northeast Sudan and southwest Yemen as the Afar mantle plume hit the base of Africa's lithosphere.
About 350,000 cubic kilometres of lava erupted around 30 million years ago.
Layer upon layer of fissure-fed lava built the flood-basalt plateau of the Ethiopian Highlands.
The eruptions coincided with the start of rifting along the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.
From 30 to 10 million years ago, shield volcanoes added another 1,000–2,000 m on top.

conflicts.note: Oligocene page (cites 2017): emplacement spread over 31–26 Ma

title: Red Sea and Gulf of Aden rifting begins

facts.text: The Arabian plate, part of the African plate for most of the Phanerozoic, began to split away in the Oligocene.
Rifting of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden began around 30 million years ago, alongside the Ethiopian flood basalts.
Rifting began in the southern Red Sea in the mid Oligocene and spread along the whole Red Sea–Gulf of Suez system in the late Oligocene.
The Gulf of Suez Rift was active from about 28 million years ago to the end of the Miocene.

conflicts.note: Arabian plate page: Africa and Arabia separated about 25 Ma

facts.text: Extension in the Rio Grande rift began about 30 million years ago.
An intense phase of rifting on low-angle faults lasted from 30 to 20 million years ago.

title: San Andreas Fault begins to form

facts.text: The San Andreas Fault began to form about 30 million years ago, as the Pacific–Farallon spreading ridge reached North America's subduction zone.
The arrival of the Murray and Mendocino fracture zones at the subduction zone started strike-slip motion and Basin and Range extension.
It also ended volcanism south of the Cascades and rotated many western North American terranes clockwise.
The first ridge segment entered the subduction zone near Baja California about 28 million years ago.

conflicts.note: Paleogene page (cites 2017, 2016): first ridge segment enters the trench near Baja California

facts.text: Dominican amber, 30–10 million years old, is nearly always clear and rich in inclusions, allowing a detailed reconstruction of a vanished tropical forest.
The eruption that formed La Garita Caldera in Colorado was among the largest and most powerful known in Earth's history.
It blasted out the Fish Canyon Tuff, about 5,000 cubic kilometres of ash-flow deposit, and the caldera formed by collapse.
It was one of many calderas of a huge ignimbrite flare-up across Colorado, Utah and Nevada from 40 to 18 million years ago.
Sanidine crystals from the tuff, astronomically dated to 28.175 million years, are a reference standard for argon–argon dating.

title: Drake Passage opens south of South America

facts.text: Seafloor spreading along the Scotia Ridge finally parted South America from Antarctica by 28 million years ago, forming the Drake Passage.
South America became an island continent and drifted north toward North America.
Published estimates for the opening range from 49 to 17 million years ago; one study finds deep-water flow possible by about 31 million years ago.
Together with the Tasmanian Gateway, the opening reshaped Oligocene ocean currents.
It may have helped trigger Antarctic glaciation, though models suggest falling carbon dioxide mattered more.

contested_note: Sources disagree on when the passage opened, from the early Eocene to the Miocene, and on whether it happened at the start or near the end of the Oligocene.

facts.text: The first pelicans appear in the fossil record about 28 million years ago.
Paraceratherium appears in the fossil record about 28 million years ago; it was the largest land mammal that ever lived.
This hornless rhino relative weighed up to 15–20 tonnes; giant indricotheres like it stood up to 6 metres at the shoulder in Eurasia.
They bucked a general trend for Oligocene mammals to be much smaller than Eocene ones.

title: Caviomorph rodents diversify in South America

facts.text: Caviomorph rodents reached Patagonia by the early Oligocene and by the Late Oligocene had split into all four main lineages.
Some grew large and competed with native hoofed mammals, perhaps helping their slow decline after the early Oligocene.

title: First cats (Proailurus)

facts.text: The first felid, Proailurus, arose in Asia in the late Oligocene and spread to Europe.
Timelines date the first cats to about 30 or 25 million years ago.
The earliest felid fossils, such as Proailurus, come from Oligocene Europe; the first cat with saber-tooth features is the Miocene Pseudaelurus.

facts.text: Elephantimorphs, the proboscidean group that includes mastodons and modern elephants, first appeared in the Late Oligocene.
One timeline dates the first true elephants to about 26 million years ago.

title: West Antarctic Ice Sheet first forms

facts.text: The West Antarctic Ice Sheet first formed about 27 million years ago, probably fed partly by glaciers from the older East Antarctic Ice Sheet.
It is a marine ice sheet: most of its ice rests on rock and sediment well below sea level, which would be ocean floor without the ice.

verification.title: Ice sheet–free West Antarctica during peak early Oligocene glaciation
verification.note: The paper finds no West Antarctic Ice Sheet at 33.7–33.2 Ma, consistent with it first forming later, around 27 Ma.

facts.text: The late Oligocene, 26.5 to 24 million years ago, probably warmed despite low carbon dioxide, though the change varied by region.
Global temperatures rose slightly but stayed well below earlier Paleogene levels, and Antarctica stayed heavily glaciated.
Pollen from the Tibetan Plateau records the warming.
Lanternfish, until then confined to shelf seas, spread into the open ocean during the warm interval at the end of the Oligocene.

verification.title: The enigma of Oligocene climate and global surface temperature evolution
verification.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
verification.note: The abstract's 34 Ma refers to the start of Antarctic glaciation, not the late Oligocene warming.

title: Farallon Plate breaks into Cocos and Nazca plates

facts.text: About 26 million years ago the Farallon Plate broke up into the Cocos and Nazca plates.
Subduction sped up, reviving volcanism in the Central Andes and broadening the volcanic arc to about 250 km.
Volcanic activity rose sharply along the Andes, and the modern volcanic arc and tectonic regime took shape.
At the Paleogene–Neogene boundary, Pacific–Farallon spreading stopped and the plate split again into today's Nazca and Cocos plates.

facts.text: Around 25.8 million years ago, the South Asian monsoon intensified sharply as the Tibetan Plateau rose.
Tibetan pollen shows the monsoon had already developed by the late Oligocene.

title: Earliest ape and Old World monkey fossils

facts.text: Tanzania's Nsungwe Formation in the Rukwa Rift, about 25.2 million years old, yields Rukwapithecus, interpreted as the earliest known ape (hominoid).
The same beds hold Nsungwepithecus, an early Old World monkey, so apes and Old World monkeys had already split by then.
That fits molecular estimates of the split at about 25–30 million years ago, though early catarrhine relationships remain uncertain.
The finds extend both groups into a poorly sampled interval; tectonic changes in East Africa may have influenced their diversification.

conflicts.note: molecular estimate for the ape–monkey divergence

title: Central America starts to close its seaway

facts.text: By the Oligocene, the Central American volcanic arc began colliding with northwestern South America.
The collision that closed the Central American Seaway started about 25 million years ago.

verification.title: How old is the Isthmus of Panama?

facts.text: Riversleigh in Queensland, Australia's most famous fossil site, preserves fossils from the late Oligocene on; some are 25 million years old.
Its limestones formed in what was once a very wet rainforest.

conflicts.note: Riversleigh page: Faunal Zone A spans the Late Oligocene

title: Sea of Japan begins to open

facts.text: Around 25 million years ago the Sea of Japan began to open, separating Japan from the mainland and forming today's island arc.

title: East African Rift begins to open

facts.text: The East African Rift began to develop around the start of the Miocene, 25–22 million years ago.
Rifting and volcanism began in northern Kenya around 30 million years ago, reaching southern Kenya by 12 and northern Tanzania by 8 million years ago.
Volcanism started on the central Ethiopian plateau around 30 million years ago, long before rifting.
Mount Elgon, at least 24 million years old, is East Africa's oldest known extinct volcano.

conflicts.note: Gregory Rift page (cites 2011): rifting and volcanism in northern Kenya

facts.text: The earliest pinnipeds, the seal group, appeared about 24 million years ago, near the end of the Oligocene.
From the Oligocene on, nautiloids vanished from each region as pinnipeds appeared there.
At the end of the Oligocene, creodonts died out everywhere except Africa and the Middle East.
A deep glaciation lasting 400,000 years at the Oligocene–Miocene boundary is recorded at McMurdo Sound and King George Island, Antarctica.
The boundary is set not at one clear global event but at regional shifts from the warmer late Oligocene to the cooler Miocene.
The Miocene opened with the Mi-1 cool event around 23 million years ago, during a major expansion of Antarctica's ice sheets.

conflicts.note: Miocene page: Mi-1 marks the start of the Early Miocene Cool Interval

facts.text: The pyrotheres, a South American mammal order known since the Early Eocene, have their last record at the end of the Oligocene.
They were among South America's distinctive native mammals, alongside astrapotheres, litopterns and notoungulates.
